before:
After the day, look at what actually happened. If you did the Protector action(s), not feeling better right away is information to learn from. It doesn't mean failure, because the process is dynamic. And you can ask yourself again, "What is this practice supposed to help, and how would I know if it's helping?" Not doing it is harder to figure out. Fear is the first guess, but maybe you didn't know how or why. Being worn out can stop you too, and sometimes whoever said they'd help couldn't make it. Hey, we've all been there. 🤗

(That was the end of the previous section. This paragraph is the first one under the new heading:)

Love Doesn't Have to Wait for Trust
after: The love can go first, though, before their trust is done going over your track record (they've heard what you still call yourself when you mess up, sometimes out loud). Your little one says "I don't trust you." You answer, "I believe you. And I love you."
brief:
- first paragraph of the section; the heading has just said love doesn't have to wait for trust
- sometimes the love is there for your little one, and it still feels unsafe to them
- why: love and trust got tied together, as if one has to vouch for the other
- they don't have to
length: one to three sentences, 25 to 60 words
guide_passage: Sometimes love is available and still feels unsafe because love and trust have become tied together as though one has to validate the other. They don’t.
next: The younger state can look at the grown-up life and say, “I don’t trust you.” The adult can answer, “I believe you. And I love you.” Trust is allowed to examine old promises, continuing self-attack, and failures of protection. Love does not have to wait for trust to issue a favorable verdict.
